content.title: About
content.content: An alcoholic malt beverage is a low‑alcohol drink produced by fermenting barley malt. It has a sweet‑caramel flavor, a subtle bitterness, and typically contains 0.5–5 % alcohol by volume.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Malt drinks originated in medieval Europe as an inexpensive way to produce alcohol.
In many countries they are called “malt” or “malt ale”.
Malt beverage is often used as a base for cocktails and mixed drinks.
Unlike beer, malt drinks usually lack hops, giving them a smoother, sweeter taste.
They can be non‑alcoholic or lightly alcoholic, making them popular for those seeking a mild buzz.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Malt beverages contain B1, B2 and B6 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: They provide magnesium, phosphorus and potassium, which help muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Moderate alcohol content
items.content: Small amounts may promote relaxation and improve mood.

items.title: Alcohol effects
items.content: Even low alcohol levels can lead to dependence and negatively affect liver health with regular consumption.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Malt drinks often contain significant sugar, contributing to weight gain and dental caries.

items.title: Barley/gluten allergy
items.content: People allergic to barley or gluten may experience reactions.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Serve chilled, straight or as part of cocktails. It is commonly enjoyed over ice with a slice of lemon or lime for a refreshing twist.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a cool, dark place with the container tightly sealed. After opening, store in the refrigerator and consume within 3–5 days.

beets-fresh-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Beets, fresh, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Beets are a root vegetable belonging to the Amaranthaceae family. Fresh beets have a deep red, sometimes purple hue, a mildly sweet flavor, and a firm, juicy texture. When cooked without added fat they retain most of their vitamins, minerals, and natural color.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beets contain betanin, a natural pigment that gives them their characteristic color and antioxidant properties.
Ancient cultures used beets both as food and for medicinal purposes.
Beets come in red and golden varieties, both nutritionally rich.
Beet juice is often used as a natural food coloring and in cosmetics.
In many countries beet soup (borscht) is traditional, but beets are also enjoyed boiled, roasted, or in salads.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Betanin and other polyphenols help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Nitrate compounds promote vasodilation, improving circulation and lowering blood pressure.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Provides vitamins and minerals
items.content: Beets supply vitamin C, folate, potassium, magnesium, and iron, essential for metabolism and blood formation.

items.title: Aids liver detoxification
items.content: Glucosinolates in beets help the body eliminate toxins.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Beets contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Blood sugar impact
items.content: Natural sugars can affect blood glucose levels, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergy to beets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beets can be eaten raw in salads, boiled as a side dish, roasted, steamed, or juiced. When cooking without added fat, steam or simmer in a small amount of water to preserve nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh beets in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, loosely packed in a perforated bag, for up to 2–3 weeks. Cooked beets should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Biscuit with fruit is a sweet baked treat that incorporates pieces of dried fruit (raisins, apricots, cranberries, etc.) into the dough. It features a crisp edge and a soft, aromatic interior, combining the buttery flavor of the biscuit with the natural sweetness of the fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recipes for fruit biscuits appeared in Europe in the 19th century as a way to use surplus dried fruit.
Dried fruit in biscuits retains a large portion of vitamins and minerals, especially vitamin C and potassium.
Traditionally, fruit biscuits were baked in home ovens, but today they are widely available in stores and cafés.
Different cultures use different fruit mixes: in England raisins and candied peel are common, while in Scandinavia cranberries and prunes are favored.
Fruit biscuits are often served with tea or coffee, as their sweetness balances the bitterness of the drinks.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dried fruits provide dietary fiber that supports regular bowel function and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Fruits such as cranberries and raisins are rich in polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Simple sugars in dried fruit are quickly absorbed, giving a rapid energy lift, making the biscuit a convenient snack.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fruit biscuits contain potassium, iron and vitamin K, which contribute to heart and bone health.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: The biscuit dough is typically made with butter, providing essential fatty acids when consumed in moderation.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Both the dried fruit and added sugar make the biscuit calorie‑dense; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Additive presence
items.content: Some commercial versions may contain preservatives and artificial flavors that are not suitable for everyone.

items.title: Risk of overconsumption
items.content: The crunchy texture and sweet taste can lead to eating larger amounts than intended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fruit biscuits can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to yogurt or granola, or used as a base for dessert plates. They are also convenient to pack for hikes and trips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store biscuits in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness and prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. cicla) is a leafy vegetable related to beetroot. It is cultivated in temperate regions and prized for its tender stems and large leaf blades. Raw chard has a mildly bitter, nutty flavor and a crisp texture. It is used in salads, smoothies, and as a quick‑cooked side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chard belongs to the same family as beet, spinach, and Swiss chard varieties.
Historical records show chard cultivation dating back to ancient Rome.
The green stems contain betaine, which can change the color of dishes when heated.
In some countries chard is nicknamed “Swiss mango” because of its bright green‑yellow hue.
Chard grows easily in home containers and pots.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Chard provides a high amount of vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and C
items.content: Vitamins A and C support vision, immunity, and act as antioxidants.

items.title: Contains magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals help maintain normal muscle and nerve function and regulate blood pressure.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports gut microbiota.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Chard is low in calories, making it a great addition to weight‑management diets.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Chard contains oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: As with many leafy greens, chard can retain pesticide residues; thorough washing is recommended.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to chard.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw chard can be added to salads, smoothies, wraps, and sandwiches. Stems are often sliced thinly, while the leafy part is used as greens. For a milder taste, you can briefly blanch the leaves in hot water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store chard in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel or in a perforated bag. Use within 3–5 days. Discard any leaves that become yellowed, slimy, or develop an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Cottage cheese is a fresh curd product obtained by coagulating milk and draining the whey. Fresh cheese NFS (non‑fermented fresh) is a soft cheese made from whole milk without the addition of enzymes, preserving a mild flavor and high protein content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cottage cheese is considered one of the oldest dairy foods, made already in ancient Egypt.
It is known by many names worldwide: in Russia – творог, in Poland – twaróg, in Greece – τυρί κρέμας.
NFS cheese is often used in desserts because it lacks the strong flavor of fermented cheeses.
Cottage cheese is rich in casein, a slowly digestible protein that supports muscle growth over time.
In some regions cottage cheese is served with honey and berries as a traditional breakfast.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Both cottage cheese and NFS cheese provide complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium supports bone and tooth health and plays a role in muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low in fat (in low‑fat versions)
items.content: Reduced‑fat cottage cheese contains little saturated fat, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Probiotic properties
items.content: Live cultures remaining in cottage cheese can promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: These dairy products contain vitamin B12, riboflavin, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may experience reactions when consuming cottage cheese or fresh cheese.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some NFS cheeses can be salty; individuals with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Lactose content
items.content: Cottage cheese contains lactose, so those with intolerance should choose lactose‑free options.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to growth of pathogenic bacteria, causing foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cottage cheese can be eaten plain, mixed into smoothies, oatmeal, salads, or used in baking. Fresh NFS cheese is often sliced thin for sandwiches, used as a filling for dumplings, or incorporated into desserts such as cheesecake.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cottage cheese and NFS cheese in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in an airtight container. They typically keep 5‑7 days after opening. Discard if an off‑odor or discoloration develops.

content.title: About
content.content: Steamed catfish fillet is a tender piece of low‑fat fish with a high protein content. Steaming preserves most of its nutrients, making it a healthy and flavorful option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Catfish are freshwater fish native to rivers and lakes across North America and Asia.
The flesh has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a soft texture, popular in many Asian cuisines.
Steaming retains up to 90% of B‑vitamins and minerals such as phosphorus and selenium.
Catfish can survive in low‑oxygen water thanks to specialized breathing organs that allow them to gulp air.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Catfish provides about 18‑20 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other fish, catfish contains little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: It contains beneficial omega‑3 fatty acids that promote heart and vascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Catfish supplies vitamin B12, B6 and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It is a good source of phosphorus, selenium and potassium, supporting bone health, antioxidant defense and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including catfish.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Freshwater catfish can accumulate cadmium or mercury in polluted waters; choose products from reputable sources.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient cooking can allow bacterial growth leading to food poisoning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steamed catfish fillet can be served on its own, sliced into salads, added to soups or rice dishes. It is often drizzled with soy sauce, lemon juice or fresh herbs to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fillet in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag at –18 °C, where it remains good for up to 3 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor.

toddler-formula-gerber-good-start-stage-.title: Toddler formula, Gerber Good Start, Stage 3

content.title: About
content.content: Toddler formula, Gerber Good Start, Stage 3 is a milk‑based infant formula for children 12 months and older, designed to support growth and development. It provides a balanced blend of proteins, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins, minerals, and pre‑biotics for digestive health.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Formulated for toddlers transitioning from baby foods to more solid meals.
Contains DHA and ARA – essential fatty acids important for brain and eye development.
Gerber Good Start uses a “gentle” formula technology that is easier on a toddler’s stomach.
Enriched with iron, calcium, and vitamin D to support bone health and immunity.
Each 400 g container typically lasts 2–3 weeks with daily feeding.

items.title: Supports growth and development
items.content: A balanced mix of macro‑ and micronutrients promotes normal physical growth, brain development, and visual function.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Pre‑biotics (fructooligosaccharides) help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A, C, E and zinc contribute to the body’s defense against infections.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Calcium and vitamin D work together to build strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: Complex carbohydrates and plant oils provide sustained energy release.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The formula contains cow’s milk; consult a pediatrician if an allergy is suspected.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Added sugars are present; limit intake for children prone to dental caries.

items.title: Not for infants under 12 months
items.content: Designed only for toddlers 12 months and older; younger infants should use age‑appropriate formulas.

items.title: Post‑opening storage
items.content: Quality can degrade quickly after opening; use within 30 days.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Mix one level scoop (≈30 g) with 180 ml of warm (not hot) water, stir until smooth, and serve immediately.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep in an airtight container and use within a month.

turkey-light-or-dark-meat-stewed-skin-no.title: Turkey, light or dark meat, stewed, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed turkey is tender poultry meat cooked slowly in liquid. The recipe uses both light (breast) and dark (thigh) meat, with the skin removed before cooking, resulting in a lower‑fat dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey is a traditional centerpiece for holiday meals in the United States and many European countries.
Stewing preserves most B‑vitamins, which are sensitive to high heat.
Turkey meat contains less saturated fat than beef but more protein.
Light meat (breast) is leaner, while dark meat (thigh) is richer in iron and zinc.
Removing the skin reduces the calorie content of the finished dish by about 30 %.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Stewed turkey provides a complete source of protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Skin‑less preparation and moderate use of dark meat make the dish suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in iron and zinc
items.content: Dark meat especially supplies iron for hemoglobin and zinc for immune function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: The dish does not cause a rapid spike in blood sugar, making it friendly for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked turkey may harbor Salmonella; ensure the internal temperature reaches 165 °F (74 °C).

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to turkey proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding salt or prepared broths can raise sodium levels; monitor seasoning.

items.title: Iron overload
items.content: People taking iron supplements should consider the additional iron from dark meat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed turkey can be served as a main course, sliced for salads, used in sandwiches, or added to soups and stews. It pairs well with herbs (rosemary, thyme), vegetables, and whole grains.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked stewed turkey in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for 2‑3 months. Reheat to 165 °F (74 °C) before serving.
